$$

If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{2}-{t}^{3},\,z={t}^{2}-t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2z\,i+3y\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}-2t)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(2t-3{t}^{2})\,j+(2t-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2{t}^{2}-2t)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(2t-3{t}^{2})\,j+(2t-1)\,k) \\  & =(2{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (2t-3{t}^{2})+(3{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\cdot (2t-1) \\  & =(-3{t}^{3}+5{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot (2t-1) \\  & =2t-9{t}^{2}+13{t}^{3}-6{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-9{t}^{2}+13{t}^{3}-6{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}+\frac{13}{4}{t}^{4}-\frac{6}{5}{t}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1-3+\frac{13}{4}-\frac{6}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e70a93bf-0c70-586e-8362-c72402361cae"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨0\,-{z}^{3},\,0⟩{|}_{z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\  & =⟨0,\,-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2},\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨{{0}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2}}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above." :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(x-1) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2})=2(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x+y,\,-x+y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{x+y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-x+y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2(x-1)^{2}-2(y+1)^{2}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(x+y)\cdot 2(x-1)-(-x+y)\cdot 2(y+1)-2((x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2((x+y)(1-x)+(x-y)(y+1)-(x-1)^{2}-(y+1)^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+2x-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4(-{r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-{r}^{3}+2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{[-{r}^{3}\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2\pi {r}^{3}-2\pi r)\,\text{d}r \\  & =-8\pi {[-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8\pi (-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-257fc3b0-4eee-568e-ab48-ba72ee13cf19"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-257fc3b0-4eee-568e-ab48-ba72ee13cf19" :answer-field/id #uuid "257fc3b0-4eee-568e-ab48-ba72ee13cf19" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-20c46104-aaee-5f81-87c8-e9c611ae6afd" :answer-field/choices ["answer-54da2db0-1ce1-5f93-af27-c7663a8c8354" "answer-20c46104-aaee-5f81-87c8-e9c611ae6afd" "answer-06f86a33-c575-56fe-bdb7-9730885ac9ec" "answer-c8614eac-4ce9-50b5-a743-5b04a0329efb" "answer-fe3f8a13-dd60-5d9d-81be-3575b6037de6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-54da2db0-1ce1-5f93-af27-c7663a8c8354" :answer/id #uuid "54da2db0-1ce1-5f93-af27-c7663a8c8354" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-3\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-20c46104-aaee-5f81-87c8-e9c611ae6afd" :answer/id #uuid "20c46104-aaee-5f81-87c8-e9c611ae6afd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-6\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-06f86a33-c575-56fe-bdb7-9730885ac9ec" :answer/id #uuid "06f86a33-c575-56fe-bdb7-9730885ac9ec" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c8614eac-4ce9-50b5-a743-5b04a0329efb" :answer/id #uuid "c8614eac-4ce9-50b5-a743-5b04a0329efb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fe3f8a13-dd60-5d9d-81be-3575b6037de6" :answer/id #uuid "fe3f8a13-dd60-5d9d-81be-3575b6037de6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135163 :tutorial/content "We're now ready to state the main result of the lesson: 

*Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then* 

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
= \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

This result is known as **Stokes' theorem** and can be considered a generalization of Green's theorem. Let's spend some time building some intuition behind this result.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field in $\mathbb R^3.$ Stokes' theorem states that the sum of the microscopic curls of $\mathbf F$ on the surface $S$ equals the macroscopic curl of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary $C$ of $S.$ 

![](images/30/308aec6213f8dd42c4f853078c0305901bc19568bfd5132221bd72743f4aa58a.png)

Consider the left-hand side of the above picture, and suppose we have a point $P$ that lies on $S.$ 

The magnitude of the flux of $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ through $S$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n.
$$

We can think of this quantity as the amount of "swirl" of $\mathbf F$ at $P$ that acts tangentially to $S$ at $P.$

If we sum (integrate) the flux of the curl through $S$ at every point over the entire surface $S,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf n\, \textrm{d}S
$$

which we usually write as

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

This expression gives us the left-hand side of Stokes' theorem.

Let's now look at the right-hand side of our image. The macroscopic curl is simply the circulation of $\mathbf F$ along the boundary of $S{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r
$$

Equating the sum of the microscopic curls with the circulation, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf r.
$$

Stokes' theorem can be summarized in a single picture as follows:

![](images/34/34b39be1166c0556eaad00a473684916c0725c186829f6085db1a322da29612a.png)

We can immediately deduce a remarkable fact. Notice the value of the surface integral depends only on the circulation at the boundary. Therefore, within a given vector field, if two surfaces $S_1$ and $S_2$ have the same boundary $C,$ then their respective surface integrals will be equal!

$$
\iint\limits_{S_1} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_{S_2} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135162 :tutorial/content "Calculating the circulation of a vector field along a closed, piecewise smooth curve $C$ can be time-consuming because it often requires splitting $C$ into several parts, evaluating a line integral along each one, and calculating their sum. 

However, in such cases, we can often use Stokes' theorem to reduce the amount of work required by converting this sum of line integrals to a single surface integral. 

For example, suppose that $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2 + y^2$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x = \pm 1$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Suppose also that $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \bigg\langle 0, \: \dfrac{1}{2}z^2, \: xz \bigg\rangle.
$$

Let's use Stokes' theorem to find the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$.

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the curl of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

![](images/fd/fd25c80fd757477b724b320d1941c57630ec1c64f36bdb44d4c1c70c526fa2a9.svg)

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-z,\,-z,\,0⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr & ={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2x+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2y+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/dc/dcf7ba14ac2c0f3da12efed6d539817ab1708273f5e8e665fdde14fee28bb4e3.png)

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
2\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-1}^{1} x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3 \: \textrm{d}y  \: \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 0.
$$

**Note**: Stokes theorem tells us that 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

 depends only on the circulation of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary of $S.$ Therefore, we could have evaluated our line integral by selecting *any* surface with $C$ as its bounding curve and integrating $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ over this surface." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134013 :activity/expected-seconds 1380.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

*Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then* 

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
= \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

This result is known as **Stokes' theorem** and can be considered a generalization of Green's theorem. Let's spend some time building some intuition behind this result.

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field in $\mathbb R^3.$ Stokes' theorem states that the sum of the microscopic curls of $\mathbf F$ on the surface $S$ equals the macroscopic curl of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary $C$ of $S.$ 

![](images/30/308aec6213f8dd42c4f853078c0305901bc19568bfd5132221bd72743f4aa58a.png)

Consider the left-hand side of the above picture, and suppose we have a point $P$ that lies on $S.$ 

The magnitude of the flux of $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ through $S$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n.
$$

We can think of this quantity as the amount of "swirl" of $\mathbf F$ at $P$ that acts tangentially to $S$ at $P.$

If we sum (integrate) the flux of the curl through $S$ at every point over the entire surface $S,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf n\, \textrm{d}S
$$

which we usually write as

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

This expression gives us the left-hand side of Stokes' theorem.

Let's now look at the right-hand side of our image. The macroscopic curl is simply the circulation of $\mathbf F$ along the boundary of $S{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r
$$

Equating the sum of the microscopic curls with the circulation, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf r.
$$

Stokes' theorem can be summarized in a single picture as follows:

![](images/34/34b39be1166c0556eaad00a473684916c0725c186829f6085db1a322da29612a.png)

We can immediately deduce a remarkable fact. Notice the value of the surface integral depends only on the circulation at the boundary. Therefore, within a given vector field, if two surfaces $S_1$ and $S_2$ have the same boundary $C,$ then their respective surface integrals will be equal!

$$
\iint\limits_{S_1} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_{S_2} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135162 :tutorial/content "Calculating the circulation of a vector field along a closed, piecewise smooth curve $C$ can be time-consuming because it often requires splitting $C$ into several parts, evaluating a line integral along each one, and calculating their sum. 

However, in such cases, we can often use Stokes' theorem to reduce the amount of work required by converting this sum of line integrals to a single surface integral. 

For example, suppose that $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2 + y^2$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x = \pm 1$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Suppose also that $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \bigg\langle 0, \: \dfrac{1}{2}z^2, \: xz \bigg\rangle.
$$

Let's use Stokes' theorem to find the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$.

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the curl of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

![](images/fd/fd25c80fd757477b724b320d1941c57630ec1c64f36bdb44d4c1c70c526fa2a9.svg)

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-z,\,-z,\,0⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr & ={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2x+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2y+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/dc/dcf7ba14ac2c0f3da12efed6d539817ab1708273f5e8e665fdde14fee28bb4e3.png)

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
2\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-1}^{1} x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3 \: \textrm{d}y  \: \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 0.
$$

**Note**: Stokes theorem tells us that 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

 depends only on the circulation of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary of $S.$ Therefore, we could have evaluated our line integral by selecting *any* surface with $C$ as its bounding curve and integrating $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ over this surface." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134013 :activity/expected-seconds 1380.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-1d416162-8b5b-53c3-aa15-9f678fcebfbf" :question/id #uuid "1d416162-8b5b-53c3-aa15-9f678fcebfbf"] ["question-1d416162-8b5b-53c3-aa15-9f678fcebfbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-162229"] ["question-1d416162-8b5b-53c3-aa15-9f678fcebfbf" :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=-y\,i+x\,j$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2\,k$ for $t\in [0,2).$"] ["question-1d416162-8b5b-53c3-aa15-9f678fcebfbf" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$

along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) =  \sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + \cos (\pi t)\, \mathbf{j} + t(2-t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,2].$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r
= \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \sin (\pi t), \qquad
y = \cos (\pi t), \qquad
z = t(2-t) = 2t-t^2.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j+z\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+(2t-{t}^{2})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2(1-t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+(2t-{t}^{2})\,k\,)\cdot (\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+2(1-t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\cdot (-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))+(2t-{t}^{2})\cdot 2(1-t) \\  & =\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+2(2t-{t}^{2})(1-t) \\  & =\pi ({cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t))+2(2t-3{t}^{2}+{t}^{3}) \\  & =\pi +4t-6{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\pi +4t-6{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\pi t+2{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[2\pi +8-16+8]-[0] \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050773} {:db/id 17592186134129 :question/id #uuid "73fef5f2-e793-56dc-a75a-943258eb19b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-161925"} {:db/id 17592186134133 :question/id #uuid $$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}},
$$

where $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} = \langle -xz, \: -yz, \: x+z^2 \rangle,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ and the plane $z=1.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above." :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ and the plane $z=1.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z = g(x,y) = 1.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-xz,\,-yz,\,{z}^{2}+x⟩{|}_{z=1} \\  & =⟨{{-x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{1+x}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\cdot 0-(-y)\cdot 0+1+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+x)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Now, note that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ of radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x = r \cos\theta, \qquad
y = r \sin\theta, \qquad
\textrm{d}A = r \, \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1+x)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }r+{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[r\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\pi r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi [{r}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048253} {:db/id 17592186049084} {:db/id 17592186134130 :question/id #uuid "ee52e831-6d2f-5771-b93b-7f7fa07dc36b" :question/math-academy-id "q-161926"} {:db/id 17592186134131 {:db/id 17592186135162 :tutorial/content "Calculating the circulation of a vector field along a closed, piecewise smooth curve $C$ can be time-consuming because it often requires splitting $C$ into several parts, evaluating a line integral along each one, and calculating their sum. 

However, in such cases, we can often use Stokes' theorem to reduce the amount of work required by converting this sum of line integrals to a single surface integral. 

For example, suppose that $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2 + y^2$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x = \pm 1$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Suppose also that $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \bigg\langle 0, \: \dfrac{1}{2}z^2, \: xz \bigg\rangle.
$$

Let's use Stokes' theorem to find the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$.

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the curl of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2}{z}^{2} & xz\end{aligned}|
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-z,\,-z,\,0⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr & ={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2x+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2y+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/dc/dcf7ba14ac2c0f3da12efed6d539817ab1708273f5e8e665fdde14fee28bb4e3.png)

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
2\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-1}^{1} x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3 \: \textrm{d}y  \: \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 0.
$$

**Note**: Stokes theorem tells us that 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

 depends only on the circulation of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary of $S.$ Therefore, we could have evaluated our line integral by selecting *any* surface with $C$ as its bounding curve and integrating $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ over this surface." :tutorial/id #uuid "fe8c7f62-0786-58b3-874d-2aca76ef3ad7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7700 :tutorial/title "Using Stokes' Theorem to Evaluate Line Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "b2a1a0ff-e72c-5813-8d4e-f400e76cbbcb" :step/math-academy-id 44684 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134929}} {:db/id 17592186134932 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135163 :tutorial/content "We're now ready to state the main result of the lesson: 

> *Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then*
> 
> 
> $$
> \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
> = \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
> $$

This result is known as **Stokes' theorem** and can be considered a generalization of Green's theorem. Let's spend some time building some intuition behind this result.

Take a moment to compare this to Green's theorem. 

Stokes' theorem is seen as an analog of Green's theorem because it relates an integral of the "derivatives" of [math]\mathbf{F}[/math] over a domain [math]S[/math] to the integral of [math]\mathbf{F}[/math] along the boundary of [math]S.[/math]

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field in $\mathbb R^3.$ Stokes' theorem states that the sum of the microscopic curls of $\mathbf F$ on the surface $S$ equals the macroscopic curl of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary $C$ of $S.$ 

![](images/30/308aec6213f8dd42c4f853078c0305901bc19568bfd5132221bd72743f4aa58a.png)

Consider the left-hand side of the above picture, and suppose we have a point $P$ that lies on $S.$ 

The magnitude of the flux of $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ through $S$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n.
$$

We can think of this quantity as the amount of "swirl" of $\mathbf F$ at $P$ that acts tangentially to $S$ at $P.$

If we sum (integrate) the flux of the curl through $S$ at every point over the entire surface $S,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf n\, \textrm{d}S
$$

which we usually write as

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

This expression gives us the left-hand side of Stokes' theorem.

Let's now look at the right-hand side of our image. The macroscopic curl is simply the circulation of $\mathbf F$ along the boundary of $S{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r
$$

Equating the sum of the microscopic curls with the circulation, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf r.
$$

Stokes' theorem can be summarized in a single picture as follows:

![](images/34/34b39be1166c0556eaad00a473684916c0725c186829f6085db1a322da29612a.png)

We can immediately deduce a remarkable fact. Notice the value of the surface integral depends only on the circulation at the boundary. Therefore, within a given vector field, if two surfaces $S_1$ and $S_2$ have the same boundary $C,$ then their respective surface integrals will be equal!

$$
\iint\limits_{S_1} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_{S_2} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f145e410-13a4-5cdd-ad1d-ba95177d8355" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7709 :tutorial/title "Stokes' Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "f2180bbb-1f4c-5c73-b6d2-6adfe5adde9f" :step/math-academy-id 44722 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134930}} {:db/id 17592186134937 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135168 :tutorial/content "The **circulation** $\Gamma$ of a three-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ along a closed, piecewise-smooth curve $C \in \mathbb R^3$ parametrized by $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b]$ is given by

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

This is the same definition as the two-dimensional case. Also, like the two-dimensional case, $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a closed curve $C,$ traversed once.

Remember that circulation is always measured with respect to our chosen orientation for $C$ (positive or negative).

For example, if we select the upward-pointing unit normal vector shown below, the positive orientation is *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

17592186134931}} {:db/id 17592186134931 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135162 :tutorial/content "Calculating the circulation of a vector field along a closed, piecewise smooth curve $C$ can be time-consuming because it often requires splitting $C$ into several parts, evaluating a line integral along each one, and calculating their sum. 

However, in such cases, we can often use Stokes' theorem to reduce the amount of work required by converting this sum of line integrals to a single surface integral. 

For example, suppose that $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z=x^2 + y^2$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x = \pm 1$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Suppose also that $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \bigg\langle 0, \: \dfrac{1}{2}z^2, \: xz \bigg\rangle.
$$

Let's use Stokes' theorem to find the circulation of $\mathbf{F}$ along $C$.

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}
= \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

By computing the curl of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2}{z}^{2} & xz\end{aligned}|
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-z,\,-z,\,0⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr & ={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2x+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 2y+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/dc/dcf7ba14ac2c0f3da12efed6d539817ab1708273f5e8e665fdde14fee28bb4e3.png)

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
2\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-1}^{1} x^3 + x^2 y + x y^2 + y^3 \: \textrm{d}y  \: \textrm{d}x = 0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = 0.
$$

**Note**: Stokes theorem tells us that 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

 depends only on the circulation of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary of $S.$ Therefore, we could have evaluated our line integral by selecting *any* surface with $C$ as its bounding curve and integrating $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ over this surface." :tutorial/id #uuid "fe8c7f62-0786-58b3-874d-2aca76ef3ad7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7700 :tutorial/title "Using Stokes' Theorem to Evaluate Line Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "b2a1a0ff-e72c-5813-8d4e-f400e76cbbcb" :step/math-academy-id 44684 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134929}} {:db/id 17592186135162 :tutorial/content "Calculating the circulation of a vector field along a closed, piecewise smooth curve $C$ can be time-consuming because it often requires splitting $C$ into several parts, evaluating a line integral along each one, and calculating their sum.

> *Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then*
> 
> 
> $$
> \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
> = \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
> $$

This result is known as **Stokes' theorem** and can be considered a generalization of Green's theorem. Let's spend some time building some intuition behind this result.

Take a moment to compare this to Green's theorem. 

Stokes' theorem is seen as an analog of Green's theorem because it relates an integral of the "derivatives" of [math]\mathbf{F}[/math] over a domain [math]S[/math] to the integral of [math]\mathbf{F}[/math] along the boundary of [math]S.[/math]

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field in $\mathbb R^3.$ Stokes' theorem states that the sum of the microscopic curls of $\mathbf F$ on the surface $S$ equals the macroscopic curl of $\mathbf F$ at the boundary $C$ of $S.$ 

![](images/30/308aec6213f8dd42c4f853078c0305901bc19568bfd5132221bd72743f4aa58a.png)

Consider the left-hand side of the above picture, and suppose we have a point $P$ that lies on $S.$ 

The magnitude of the flux of $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ through $S$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n.
$$

We can think of this quantity as the amount of "swirl" of $\mathbf F$ at $P$ that acts tangentially to $S$ at $P.$

If we sum (integrate) the flux of the curl through $S$ at every point over the entire surface $S,$ we get

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf n\, \textrm{d}S
$$

which we usually write as

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

This expression gives us the left-hand side of Stokes' theorem.

Let's now look at the right-hand side of our image. The macroscopic curl is simply the circulation of $\mathbf F$ along the boundary of $S{:}$

$$
\oint\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r
$$

Equating the sum of the microscopic curls with the circulation, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \oint\limits_C\mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf r.
$$

Stokes' theorem can be summarized in a single picture as follows:

![](images/34/34b39be1166c0556eaad00a473684916c0725c186829f6085db1a322da29612a.png)

We can immediately deduce a remarkable fact. Notice the value of the surface integral depends only on the circulation at the boundary. Therefore, within a given vector field, if two surfaces $S_1$ and $S_2$ have the same boundary $C,$ then their respective surface integrals will be equal!

$$
\iint\limits_{S_1} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_{S_2} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f145e410-13a4-5cdd-ad1d-ba95177d8355" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7709 :tutorial/title "Stokes' Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "f2180bbb-1f4c-5c73-b6d2-6adfe5adde9f" :step/math-academy-id 44722 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134930}} {:db/id 17592186135163 :tutorial/content "We're now ready to state the main result of the lesson:

$$
\Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t.
$$

This is the same definition as the two-dimensional case. Also, like the two-dimensional case, $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a closed curve $C,$ traversed once.

Remember that circulation is always measured with respect to our chosen orientation for $C$ (positive or negative).

Let's get some practice at computing circulation over three-dimensional curves." :tutorial/id #uuid "fa33c72b-b304-5717-a1ca-c81df764530f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7754 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186135169 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have an oriented surface $S$ (not closed) whose **boundary curve** is the closed curve $C,$ as shown below. 

![](images/bc/bc0ac6b400535839d3571d61c07f3ac752bc4e85020f9b3e4cc08410b0023822.png)

Whenever we select an orientation for $S,$ our chosen orientation automatically induces a positive orientation for $C.$

For example, if we select the upward-pointing unit normal vector shown below, the positive orientation is *counterclockwise* when viewed from above.

![](images/73/7353d1a742e374e3704155e8c99cc26c62e8486f3606cba1144c35871ad3c432.png)

Assume that you are standing on the curve $C$ with your head pointing upward (i.e., in the same direction as $\mathbf n$). Then, if you traverse $C$ in the positive direction, the surface will always be on your left.

For example, if $z=f(x,y)$ is upward-oriented, the projection of the bounding curve onto the $xy$-plane runs counterclockwise when viewed from above. 

![](images/e9/e948c13c040a01ce46b6f715e313c8aabb2634e5871739169dd3f38e3229e768.png)

Now, suppose we select the opposite orientation for $\mathbf n,$ shown below.

![](images/81/81d5e3126c07f30b68bd2d46c4104212f6c7edf34baf65b077ad297f224ebe8a.png)

By choosing the *opposite* orientation for $\mathbf n,$ the positive orientation for $C$ is *clockwise* when viewed from above!

If you're not convinced, grab a child's doll, a toothbrush, or any other object with some kind of head, and mark its left and right sides (be careful not to damage it!). Then, walk it around the edge of a table so that its left side is always next to the table surface. If you turn it upside down, you will see that the object must traverse the table's edge in the *opposite* direction for the table surface to stay on the left." :tutorial/id #uuid
